title: Financial Services Policy Essentials for Government
summary: A ten-module programme giving government officials a clear grounding in the financial system, regulatory architecture, international standards and the policy levers government holds.
intro: This training programme equips ministers, officials and public bodies with a clear understanding of how the financial system works, how it is regulated and the policy levers government holds over it.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give officials in finance ministries, treasuries and other public bodies a practical, non-technical grounding in the financial system, the architecture of financial regulation and the respective roles of government and independent regulators. Participants leave able to frame financial services policy, ask the right questions of regulators and industry, and represent the national interest in international standard-setting and peer review.
sections.What It Covers: How the financial system works, the economic case for regulation, regulatory architecture and models, independence and accountability of regulators, international standards and peer reviews, banking, insurance, securities and payments, financial stability, financial crime, the policy levers available to government, and designing a national financial services policy.
Intended Audience: Officials in finance ministries and treasuries responsible for financial services, banking and capital markets policy
Senior officials and advisers to ministers who oversee or appoint financial regulators
Staff of public agencies, cabinet offices and parliamentary committees who work on financial sector issues
Learning Objectives: Explain how the financial system channels savings into investment and where it can fail
Compare the main models of regulatory architecture and their strengths and weaknesses
Distinguish the roles of government and independent regulators and design effective accountability
Explain the international standards and peer review processes that apply to the national system
Identify the policy levers available to government and the trade-offs between them
Design the elements of a coherent national financial services policy
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as an intensive programme over three to four days or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a plain-language briefing with case studies and policy discussion, and modules can be selected or tailored to the ministry's priorities.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of public policy or economic affairs is helpful. No technical background in finance or regulation is required.
Core Reading: BCBS (2024), Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision
IOSCO (2017), Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation
IAIS (2019), Insurance Core Principles and Common Framework for the Supervision of Internationally Active Insurance Groups
IMF (2021), Financial Sector Assessment Program Review: Towards a More Stable and Sustainable Financial System

modules.title: How the Financial System Works
modules.summary: The core functions of the financial system, the main institutions and markets that perform them, and how money, credit and risk flow through the economy.
objectives: Explain the economic functions of banks, insurers, markets and payment systems
Describe how institutions and markets connect households, firms and government
Identify the links between the financial sector, public finances and growth
syllabus: Intermediation, maturity transformation, risk transfer and payments
Banks, insurers, pension schemes, funds and non-bank lenders
Money, bond, equity and derivatives markets
The financial sector's contribution to growth, tax and employment

modules.title: Why Regulate: Market Failures and Policy Objectives
modules.summary: The economic case for financial regulation, the objectives regulators pursue, and the tensions between stability, consumer protection, market integrity, competition and growth.
objectives: Explain the market failures that justify financial regulation
Distinguish prudential, conduct, market integrity and financial crime objectives
Assess the trade-offs between regulatory objectives and economic growth
syllabus: Information asymmetry, externalities, moral hazard and contagion
Statutory objectives and how they are framed in legislation
Competition and growth objectives: benefits and risks
Lessons from crises on the cost of regulatory failure

modules.title: Regulatory Architecture: Models and Choices
modules.summary: How countries organise financial regulation, from sectoral and integrated regulators to twin peaks models, and the role of central banks, ministries and other public bodies.
objectives: Compare sectoral, integrated, twin peaks and hybrid models
Explain the role of the central bank in prudential and macroprudential policy
Evaluate coordination arrangements between authorities
syllabus: Sectoral, integrated and twin peaks models compared
Central banks, financial stability committees and deposit insurers
Memoranda of understanding and inter-agency coordination
Case studies of architecture reform after a crisis

modules.title: Independence and Accountability of Regulators
modules.summary: Why regulators are made operationally independent, the safeguards that protect independence, and how government and legislators hold regulators to account without undermining it.
objectives: Explain the rationale for operational independence and the risks of political interference
Design governance, appointment, funding and legal protection arrangements
Apply accountability tools such as reporting, performance review and parliamentary scrutiny
syllabus: Independence in international standards: what is expected
Board composition, appointments, dismissal and funding models
Annual reports, remit letters, performance frameworks and audit
Questions government should ask its regulators

modules.title: International Standards, Standard-Setters and Peer Reviews
modules.summary: The international bodies that set financial standards, how those standards bind or influence national policy, and how assessments and peer reviews judge a country's framework.
objectives: Describe the roles of the G20, FSB, BCBS, IOSCO, IAIS, CPMI and FATF
Explain how standards are developed and how government can influence them
Prepare for IMF and World Bank assessments, FSB peer reviews and FATF evaluations
syllabus: The international financial architecture and its standard-setters
Core principles for banking, insurance, securities and market infrastructure
Financial sector assessments, peer reviews and mutual evaluations
Implementing recommendations and managing reputational consequences

modules.title: Banking, Insurance and Prudential Regulation
modules.summary: How banks and insurers are regulated for safety and soundness, what capital and liquidity rules aim to achieve, and the policy choices government faces in implementing them.
objectives: Explain the purpose of capital, liquidity and solvency requirements
Assess proportionality choices for smaller and domestic institutions
Identify the fiscal and growth implications of prudential policy
syllabus: Capital, leverage and liquidity standards for banks
Solvency and policyholder protection for insurers
Proportionality, local adaptation and timing of implementation
Credit supply, lending to the economy and the cost of prudential rules

modules.title: Capital Markets, Conduct and Consumer Protection
modules.summary: How securities markets, investment services and retail financial products are regulated, and the policy choices in balancing investor protection, market access and innovation.
objectives: Explain the regulation of issuers, intermediaries, funds and trading venues
Describe conduct and consumer protection frameworks and redress mechanisms
Assess where conduct failures create political and fiscal pressure
syllabus: Securities regulation: disclosure, market abuse and intermediaries
Retail investor protection, suitability and product governance
Complaints, ombudsman schemes and compensation arrangements
Case studies of mis-selling scandals and the policy response

modules.title: Financial Stability, Crisis Management and Financial Crime
modules.summary: The macroprudential framework, how failing institutions are resolved, and the national arrangements for combating money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions evasion.
objectives: Explain systemic risk and the macroprudential tools available to authorities
Describe resolution regimes, deposit insurance and the role of the finance ministry in a crisis
Identify government's responsibilities for AML/CFT and sanctions
syllabus: Systemic risk, macroprudential tools and financial stability committees
Resolution, bail-in, deposit insurance and the limits of public support
National AML/CFT strategy, FATF standards and the national FIU
Financial sanctions: implementation and enforcement

modules.title: Policy Levers and Policy Design
modules.summary: The instruments government holds over the financial sector, from legislation and regulatory remits to tax, public ownership and market development, and how to design and evaluate policy using them.
objectives: Identify the legislative, fiscal, institutional and convening levers available
Apply cost-benefit analysis and consultation to financial services policy
Evaluate industry proposals and lobbying with appropriate scepticism
syllabus: Legislation, secondary rules and remit letters
Tax policy, public guarantees, state-owned institutions and development banks
Impact assessment, consultation and post-implementation review
Managing industry engagement and avoiding regulatory capture

modules.title: Designing a National Financial Services Policy
modules.summary: Brings the programme together by examining how a national financial services strategy is developed, how emerging issues are anticipated and how policy is translated into action.
objectives: Assess the national financial sector's strengths, vulnerabilities and priorities
Anticipate emerging issues including digital assets, AI, climate and cyber risk
Produce a policy action plan with clear roles for government and regulators
syllabus: Diagnosing the financial sector: evidence, data and assessments
Emerging issues: digital assets, AI, sustainable finance and operational resilience
Sequencing reforms and building institutional capacity
Workshop: a national financial services policy action plan

related.title: Building a Competitive Financial Centre: Strategy, Regulation and Investment Promotion
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping ministries and investment promotion agencies build a competitive, reputable financial centre and measure the results.

related.title: Drafting Financial Services Legislation
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping legislative drafters and legal advisers design and draft effective, enforceable and technology-neutral financial services legislation.

related.title: Financial Crises and Public Finances: Crisis Preparedness for Government
related.summary: An eight-module advanced programme preparing finance ministries and senior officials to manage financial crises, protect public finances and coordinate resolution.

related.title: Financial Services Regulation: A Briefing Programme for Parliamentarians
related.summary: A six-module, non-technical briefing programme helping parliamentarians and committee staff scrutinise financial legislation and hold regulators to account.

related.title: AI in Financial Services: Policy Choices for Government
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping policymakers understand AI in financial services and make informed choices on regulation, institutional roles and national strategy.

related.title: Developing Capital Markets and Investment Fund Industries
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping policymakers develop deep, well-regulated capital markets and fund industries through credible, well-sequenced reform.
